description: How geological events become hazards and what controls the level of risk.
content_html:
What Makes a Geological Event a Hazard?

Not every earthquake or volcanic eruption causes widespread harm. A geological event only becomes a hazard when people or infrastructure lie in its path. The same magnitude earthquake that passes unnoticed beneath an uninhabited ocean floor can devastate a densely populated city. Understanding this distinction is central to the way geologists study risk.

Two factors determine the level of risk: the hazard probability and the vulnerability of the population. A sparsely populated, well-prepared nation facing a moderate eruption may suffer far fewer casualties than a densely populated, under-resourced community facing a smaller event. Geologists use the term risk to describe this combination: risk = hazard probability × vulnerability.

Key Fact

The level of risk from a geological hazard is shaped by population density, level of economic development (LEDC versus MEDC), quality of education, and the effectiveness of communication systems and early warning schemes.

Earthquakes

Earthquakes occur when stress built up along faults is suddenly released, sending seismic waves radiating outward from the focus. Shaking at the surface is strongest directly above the focus, at a point called the epicentre. Earthquake intensity is described using the Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale (I to XII), which measures observed effects — from barely felt tremors at intensity I, through structural damage at V–VII, to total devastation at XII. The Richter scale (and its modern replacement, the moment magnitude scale) measures the energy released: it is logarithmic, so a magnitude 7 earthquake releases roughly 32 times more energy than a magnitude 6.

Secondary hazards from earthquakes include liquefaction — where waterlogged sediment temporarily behaves like a liquid — and landslides triggered by ground shaking on steep slopes. In coastal areas or under the ocean, earthquakes can displace the sea bed and generate tsunamis. The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake (magnitude 9.0) off Japan showed how a single event can combine ground shaking, structural collapse, tsunami run-up and a nuclear emergency into an overlapping cascade of hazards.

The Mercalli scale is qualitative — it records what people experienced and what damage occurred, so it varies from place to place for the same earthquake. The Richter (or moment magnitude) scale is quantitative — it gives a single number representing the total energy released at the source. Examiners regularly ask students to explain both. Remember: Mercalli describes effects; moment magnitude describes energy. A useful check — can a location 200 km from the epicentre have a different Mercalli intensity than a location 20 km away? Yes. Can it have a different Richter magnitude? No.

Volcanic Eruptions

Volcanic hazards depend heavily on the composition of the magma. Low-viscosity basaltic magma (common at divergent boundaries and hot spots) allows gases to escape gradually, producing effusive eruptions with fast-moving lava flows. High-viscosity rhyolitic or andesitic magma (common at subduction zones) traps gases, building pressure until explosive eruptions blast out ash clouds and pyroclastic flows — fast-moving mixtures of hot gas, ash and rock fragments that travel at speeds exceeding 100 km per hour and reach temperatures above 700°C. Pyroclastic flows are among the most lethal volcanic hazards and cannot be outrun.

Additional volcanic hazards include lahars (volcanic mud flows formed when ash mixes with water from ice melt or rainfall), tephra fall (solid material ejected into the atmosphere), and volcanic gases such as sulfur dioxide, which can cause acid rain and respiratory problems far downwind. The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) measures eruption size on a logarithmic scale from 0 (non-explosive) to 8 (super-eruption). The 1980 Mount St Helens eruption was VEI 5; the 1991 Pinatubo eruption was VEI 6.

Key Fact

Pyroclastic flows are the most dangerous volcanic hazard. They travel faster than 100 km per hour, reach temperatures above 700°C, and can travel downhill in any direction. Lava flows are slower and more predictable, allowing evacuation time.

Landslides and Subsidence

A landslide occurs when the driving force of gravity on a slope exceeds the resistance provided by the strength of the material and friction. Triggers include earthquake shaking, volcanic activity loading slopes with ash and lava, heavy rainfall saturating soils, and undercutting by rivers or coastal erosion. Landslides can bury settlements, block rivers to form lakes that burst, and trigger secondary tsunamis if they enter the sea. Subsidence — the gradual sinking of the ground surface — can result from the withdrawal of groundwater or hydrocarbons, from dissolving limestone (creating sinkholes), or from mining.

Less economically developed countries (LEDCs) typically have weaker building regulations, fewer resources to enforce them, less access to early warning technology, lower levels of public education about hazards, and less developed emergency response infrastructure. The 2010 Haiti earthquake (magnitude 7.0) killed around 230,000 people, while a similarly sized earthquake in the United States or Japan would likely kill far fewer because of stricter building codes and better preparedness. MEDCs can invest in seismic engineering, real-time monitoring networks, and public evacuation drills — all of which reduce vulnerability even when the hazard probability stays the same.

Tsunamis

Tsunamis are generated when a large volume of water is suddenly displaced — most commonly by a submarine earthquake along a subduction zone, but also by submarine landslides or volcanic caldera collapse. In the open ocean, tsunami waves are long (hundreds of kilometres) and low (less than 1 metre high), travelling at speeds approaching 800 km per hour. As the wave enters shallow coastal water it slows, causing its height to increase dramatically — a process called shoaling. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, triggered by a magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra, generated waves exceeding 30 metres in parts of Aceh province, Indonesia, killing over 230,000 people across 14 countries. The geological context is key: the tsunami was caused by sudden vertical movement of the sea floor at the convergent boundary between the Indo-Australian and Eurasian plates.
exam_tip_html: When answering a 6-mark extended response question about hazards, make sure you explain why a factor increases risk, not just list it. For example, do not just write “LEDCs are more vulnerable” — explain that weaker building regulations, less warning infrastructure and poorer emergency services amplify the death toll. For compare questions, always describe both features in each point: “Pyroclastic flows travel faster than 100 km/h and cannot be outrun, whereas lava flows move slowly enough to allow evacuation.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A geological event becomes a hazard only when it threatens people or infrastructure; risk depends on both the probability of the event and the vulnerability of the population.
  • Earthquakes generate hazards through shaking, liquefaction, landslides and tsunamis; their size is measured on the logarithmic moment magnitude scale and their effects by the Mercalli scale.
  • Volcanic hazards range from slow lava flows to lethal pyroclastic flows and lahars; explosive eruptions from high-viscosity magma pose the greatest risk and are rated on the VEI scale.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the Richter (moment magnitude) scale?
A) It measures the effects observed at different locations for a single earthquake
B) It measures the energy released at the earthquake source on a logarithmic scale
C) It measures the depth of the earthquake focus in kilometres
D) It measures the duration of ground shaking at the surface
practice_questions.marks: B) It measures the energy released at the earthquake source on a logarithmic scale [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the type of volcanic hazard that consists of a fast-moving mixture of hot gas, ash and rock fragments.
Describe two ways in which a lahar (volcanic mud flow) can form.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for any two of:
- Hot ash and rock debris mix with rainfall on the volcano's slopes, forming a fast-moving mud flow.
- Volcanic heat melts snow or ice near the summit, releasing large volumes of water that mix with loose ash and debris.
- Eruption material enters a river or lake, incorporating the water into a rapidly flowing slurry.
[2 marks total]

practice_questions.text: A tsunami wave travels 3,200 km across the open ocean in 4 hours. Calculate the average speed of the wave in km per hour. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Speed = distance / time = 3,200 / 4 = 800 km/h [2 marks: 1 for correct method/working, 1 for correct answer with units]
Note: accept 800 km h⁻¹

practice_questions.text: Explain why a magnitude 7 earthquake in a less economically developed country (LEDC) often causes more casualties than a magnitude 7 earthquake in a more economically developed country (MEDC).
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- LEDCs typically have weaker or unenforced building regulations, so structures collapse more easily under seismic shaking. (1)
- LEDCs have fewer resources to install and maintain monitoring or early warning systems, so residents receive less warning to evacuate. (1)
- Emergency response capacity is lower in LEDCs — fewer trained rescue workers, less equipment, and less developed road networks slow recovery and increase the death toll. (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the view that volcanic eruptions pose a greater hazard to human populations than earthquakes. In your answer, discuss evidence both for and against this view and reach a conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation using specific hazard types and real examples; considers factors such as predictability, speed of onset, spatial extent and secondary hazards for both; well-reasoned conclusion.
Secure: Clear discussion of both hazard types with two or more developed comparisons; conclusion present but may be partially justified.
Developing: Some relevant points about both hazard types but comparison is limited or one-sided; conclusion may be absent.
Emerging: Simple points about one hazard type with little or no comparison; conclusion absent.

Points in support (volcanoes more hazardous):
- Pyroclastic flows travel at over 100 km/h and are unsurvivable, whereas many earthquake zones have hours of warning from foreshocks or P-wave detectors.
- Lahars, tephra fall and gas emissions create cascading hazards lasting days to years after an eruption.
- Volcanic ash disrupts agriculture, water supplies and air travel over vast areas.

Points against (earthquakes more hazardous):
- Earthquakes strike without immediate precursor signs visible to the public and can trigger tsunamis affecting multiple countries simultaneously (e.g. 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, 230,000+ deaths).
- Ground shaking can destroy entire urban areas within seconds; liquefaction makes rescue harder.
- Many major cities sit on fault lines rather than near active volcanoes.

Conclusion: The relative risk depends on location, population density and preparedness. Neither hazard type is universally more dangerous — a well-monitored stratovolcano with evacuation plans in place may be less hazardous in practice than an unexpected earthquake striking a densely populated city with poor building standards. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What does the Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale measure?
options: The total energy released at the earthquake source
The depth of the earthquake focus underground
The effects and damage observed at different locations
The frequency of seismic waves reaching the surface

knowledge_checks.q: What type of magma is most likely to produce an explosive volcanic eruption?
options: Fluid magma rich in iron and magnesium
Cool magma with few dissolved gases

knowledge_checks.q: A tsunami is generated when a large volume of water is suddenly _____, most commonly by a submarine earthquake.
The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) is a _____ scale used to measure the size of a volcanic eruption.
Match each geological hazard to its key characteristic:
right: A fast-moving mixture of volcanic gas, ash and rock exceeding 100 km/h
A volcanic mud flow formed when ash mixes with water
A series of large ocean waves caused by sudden sea-floor displacement

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between the Mercalli scale and the moment magnitude (Richter) scale?
flashcard_questions.a: Mercalli measures observed effects at each location; moment magnitude measures total energy released at the source.

flashcard_questions.q: What geological setting produces the most explosive volcanic eruptions?
flashcard_questions.a: Subduction zones, where high-viscosity andesitic or rhyolitic magma traps gases.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are pyroclastic flows more lethal than lava flows?
flashcard_questions.a: They travel faster than 100 km/h and reach over 700°C, making escape impossible.
A volcanic mud flow formed when ash and rock debris mix with water from rain or melting ice.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the focus (hypocentre) of an earthquake?
flashcard_questions.a: The point underground where the earthquake originates and energy is first released.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a tsunami wave behave as it reaches shallow coastal water?
flashcard_questions.a: It slows down and its height increases dramatically, a process called shoaling.

flashcard_questions.q: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami was triggered by an earthquake at which plate boundary?
flashcard_questions.a: The convergent boundary between the Indo-Australian and Eurasian plates, off Sumatra.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do LEDCs typically suffer more casualties from earthquakes than MEDCs of similar magnitude?
flashcard_questions.a: Weaker building regulations, less monitoring infrastructure and fewer trained emergency responders.

flashcard_questions.q: What does risk equal in the geological hazard equation?
What VEI rating did the 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption receive?
Name two secondary hazards triggered by earthquakes (other than tsunamis).
What causes subsidence in areas underlain by limestone?
flashcard_questions.a: Rainwater dissolves limestone along joints, creating underground cavities that collapse into sinkholes.

glossary_terms.definition: A natural event that poses a threat to people, property or the environment.
The probability that a hazard will occur in a given area within a given time period.
The degree of loss resulting from a hazard, affected by population density, wealth, building quality and preparedness.
The point underground where an earthquake originates; also called the hypocentre.
A series of large ocean waves generated by sudden displacement of the sea floor, typically caused by a submarine earthquake.
Molten rock below the Earth's surface; once it reaches the surface it is called lava.
The rapid downslope movement of rock, soil or debris under gravity, often triggered by earthquakes, volcanic activity, or heavy rainfall.
